script.heading: Intro
sentences: Welcome to Critical Care Daily for August 03, 2026.
Today we will review 2 recent ICU-relevant publications.

Use this as a morning triage tool, then open the source link for full-text appraisal before changing practice.

script.heading: Story 1 - H3.1 Nucleosomes to Predict Renal Replacement Therapy and Mort

A total of 443 patients (45.6%) presented with sepsis, and 520 patients (53.6%) had septic shock.

In a multivariable analysis for 28-day mortality, a one unit increase in log10 H3.1 levels was associated with a 48% increase in 28-day mortality (adjusted hazard ratio [HR], 1.48, 95% CI, 1.07-2.04; p = 0.02).

In a multivariable Cox regression controlling for maximum lactate, procalcitonin, and C-reactive protein levels, plasma H3.1 levels were significantly higher in patients who developed AKI requiring RRT when compared with patients who did not develop AKI, with one log10 increase of H3.1 increasing the risk of 28-day RRT by 80% (adjusted HR, 1.8; 95% CI, 1.34-2.40; p < 0.001).
For critical appraisal, focus on whether the design supports a causal conclusion and whether the patients resemble your ICU population.
The bedside implication is this: This is not yet bedside-changing; treat it as biomarker evidence that needs validation against current sepsis workflows and turnaround time.

articles.title: H3.1 Nucleosomes to Predict Renal Replacement Therapy and Mortality in Sepsis-A Secondary Analysis of the SISPCT Randomized Control Trial.
articles.summary: A secondary analysis of prospectively collected samples from the large multicenter Effect of Sodium Selenite Administration and Procalcitonin-Guided Therapy on Mortality in Patients with Severe Sepsis or Septic Shock (SISPCT) trial. A total of 971 patients with complete data on plasma H3.1 admission levels with sepsis and septic shock, and 927 patients with complete data on RRT requirements. A total of 443 patients (45.6%) presented with sepsis, and 520 patients (53.6%) had septic shock. In a multivariable analysis for 28-day mortality, a one unit increase in log10 H3.1 levels was associated with a 48% increase in 28-day mortality (adjusted hazard ratio [HR], 1.48, 95% CI, 1.07-2.04; p = 0.02). In a multivariable Cox regression controlling for maximum lactate, procalcitonin, and C-reactive protein levels, plasma H3.1 levels were significantly higher in patients who developed AKI requiring RRT when compared with patients who did not develop AKI, with one log10 increase of H3.1 increasing the risk of 28-day RRT by 80% (adjusted HR, 1.8; 95% CI, 1.34-2.40; p < 0.001).

articles.title: Renal Resistive Index Responsiveness to a Mean Arterial Pressure Test As a Guide for Mean Arterial Pressure Target in the Early Phase of Septic Shock: A Physiological Study.
articles.summary: Guidelines recommend targeting a mean arterial pressure (MAP) greater than or equal to 65 mm Hg in septic shock. Patients in the early phase of septic shock (norepinephrine ≥ 0.05 µg/kg/min base within 9 hr of initiation, with or without lactate > 2 mmol/L) without chronic kidney disease or immediate need for renal replacement therapy. RRI responders were defined by an RRI decrease greater than or equal to 0.05 during the MAP test. Following the MAP test, patients were randomized according to the "low" (65-70) or "high" (80-85 mm Hg) MAP target for 5 days, stratified by RRI response during the MAP test. Eighty patients were randomized; 23 (29%) were RRI responders.
